Projection Defined

eqdc <- '+proj=eqdc +lat_0=40 +lon_0=-96 +lat_1=20 +lat_2=60 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs'



Loading Data

# USA State Boundaries
states <- AOI::aoi_get(state = 'conus') |> st_transform(eqdc)

# Country Boundaries
countries <- AOI::aoi_get(country = c("MX", "CA", "USA")) |> st_transform(eqdc)

# Cities CSV (Download from https://simplemaps.com/data/us-cities and place in data/)
cities_df <- read_csv("data/uscities.csv")

# Convert to spatial object
cities <- st_as_sf(cities_df, coords = c("lng", "lat"), crs = 4326) |> st_transform(eqdc)




Question 2: Calculating Distances

Distance to State Borders

# Convert state boundaries to MULTILINESTRING (preserve individual borders)
state_borders <- states |> 
  st_union() |> 
  st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")

# Distance from each city to nearest state border (in km)
cities$dist_to_state <- st_distance(cities, state_borders) |> set_units("km") |> drop_units()

# Table of 5 farthest cities
cities |>
  arrange(desc(dist_to_state)) |>
  select(city, state_name, dist_to_state) |>
  head(5) |>
  flextable()

Distance to National Border

# Create national outline from states
national_outline <- states |> 
  st_union() |> 
  st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")

# Distance from each city to national border (in km)
cities$dist_to_national <- st_distance(cities, national_outline) |> set_units("km") |> drop_units()

# Table of 5 farthest cities
cities |>
  arrange(desc(dist_to_national)) |>

Question 3

Map the 3 countries, CONUS states, and the 10 largest USA cities

# Top 10 cities by population
top10 <- cities |> 
  arrange(desc(population)) |> 
  slice(1:10)

# Plot all 3 countries, states, and label top 10 cities
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = countries, fill = "gray90", color = "black", size = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, color = "darkblue", lty = 2) +
  geom_sf(data = top10, aes(size = population), color = "darkred") +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = top10, aes(label = city, geometry = geometry), stat = "sf_coordinates") +
  theme_minimal()










Color cities by distance to national border, label 5 farthest

farthest_state <- cities |> arrange(desc(dist_to_state)) |> slice(1:5)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = cities, aes(color = dist_to_state)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Distance to State Border (km)") +
  geom_sf(data = farthest_state, size = 2, color = "red") +
  geom_label_repel(data = farthest_state, aes(label = city, geometry = geometry), stat = "sf_coordinates") +
  theme_minimal()

Highlight cities ~equal distance to Canada and Mexico (±100 km diff)

# Create difference variable
cities <- cities |> 
  mutate(diff_can_mex = abs(dist_to_mexico - dist_to_canada))

equal_distance <- cities |> filter(diff_can_mex <= 100)

top5_equal <- equal_distance |> arrange(desc(population)) |> slice(1:5)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = cities, color = "gray80") +
  geom_sf(data = equal_distance, aes(color = diff_can_mex)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Difference (km)") +
  geom_sf(data = top5_equal, size = 2, color = "red") +
  geom_label_repel(data = top5_equal, aes(label = city, geometry = geometry), stat = "sf_coordinates") +
  theme_minimal()











Question 4

Identify Cities in the 100-Mile (160 km) Border Zone

# Filter cities within 160 km of the national border
cities$in_border_zone <- cities$dist_to_national <= 160

border_zone_cities <- cities |> filter(in_border_zone)



How many cities are in the zone?

nrow(border_zone_cities)

[1] 9813




What percentage of the population lives in that zone?

total_population <- sum(cities$population, na.rm = TRUE)
border_population <- sum(border_zone_cities$population, na.rm = TRUE)
percent_in_zone <- (border_population / total_population) * 100



Show results in a table

tibble(
  `Cities in Border Zone` = nrow(border_zone_cities),
  `Population in Zone` = border_population,
  `Total Population` = total_population,
  `Percent in Zone` = round(percent_in_zone, 2)
) |> flextable()

Map cities in the zone

top_10_danger <- border_zone_cities |> arrange(desc(population)) |> slice(1:10)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = cities, color = "gray90", size = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = border_zone_cities, aes(color = population)) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "orange", high = "darkred", name = "Population") +
  geom_label_repel(data = top_10_danger, aes(label = city, geometry = geometry), stat = "sf_coordinates") +
  theme_minimal()










Most populous city in each state within the danger zone

library(dplyr)

top_city_per_state <- border_zone_cities |> 
  group_by(state_name) |> 
  slice_max(order_by = population, n = 1) |> 
  ungroup()

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = border_zone_cities, aes(color = population)) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "orange", high = "darkred") +
  geom_label_repel(data = top_city_per_state, aes(label = city, geometry = geometry), stat = "sf_coordinates") +
  theme_minimal()

I found that 9,813 cities in the U.S. are within 100 miles of a border. These cities have about 216 million people, which is 53.7% of the total population in the dataset. This supports what the ACLU said — that more than half of the U.S. population lives in this “border zone.”
This matters because in this zone, the government has more power to stop and search people without a warrant. So, many people might be affected, not just in small border towns, but also in big cities like San Diego, El Paso, and Miami.
The maps showed that border zone cities are found all over near Mexico, Canada, and both coasts. We also found the most populated city in each state inside the zone, showing how wide this zone reaches across the country.
In short, this lab helped show how maps and data can help us understand how laws affect people in real places.
